turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Dr. Nova, most engineers think data cleaning just means writing a few pandas replace calls, dropping rows with weird timestamps, and running strip on strings. Why does that break in large clinical or financial pipelines?

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Consider what happens when you blindly delete every record that violates a timestamp order constraint or carries unparsed blood pressure text, Kaito! On PhysioNet MIMIC-III ICU records, naive listwise dropping discarded 64% of the entire hospital cohort!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Deleting 64% of your patients?! And even worse, if someone copied a customer name from a PDF with an invisible zero-width space U+200B inside it, Python equality and SQL joins fail silently without raising a single error!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Exactly! Declarative cleaning replaces destructive guesswork with auditable invariants: canonical byte normalization, minimum-cost repair weights, and manifold-safe donor imputation.

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Dr. Nova, why can't we run Functional Dependency and Denial Constraint checks FIRST, and clean strings afterward?

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Think about grouping records by City under a ZIP code check, Kaito! If Record 1 says S-t-a-n-f-o-r-d and Record 2 has a hidden zero-width space inside S-t-a-n-f-o-r-d, Python groupby reports two distinct cities under the same ZIP—triggering phantom violations—OR fails to group keys sharing the same noisy ZIP!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Aha! And similarly, you can't check if Systolic Blood Pressure exceeds Diastolic until regex parsing extracts 120 and 80 from free-text strings like 'BP: 120-80 mmHg'!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Precisely: canonical bytes and physical units establish clean domains first; logic constraints audit relations second; minimum-cost repair resolves conflicts third.

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Dr. Nova, walk me through an example of Bohannon's cost weights! Suppose three hospital visits share ZIP 94305: two list City as Stanford, while one lists Palo Alto.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Let us compare every consistent repair! If ZIP has confidence weight 5 and City has weight 1, option one updates just that single conflicting City from Palo Alto to Stanford at total cost 1.0.

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Whereas rewriting the other two records' Cities to Palo Alto costs 2.0, and overriding the verified ZIP code on the single row costs 5.0! So minimum-cost argmin picks 1.0 every time!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: And notice that not a single patient encounter row was deleted—all clinical vitals remain intact for downstream cohort modeling!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Dr. Nova, why do database theorists phrase constraints negatively—forbidding conjunctions—instead of writing positive if-then implications?

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Because in SQL query translation, Kaito, every negated conjunction maps one-to-one onto a direct violation-detection query! Finding rows violating ZIP implies City is literally SELECT t1, t2 WHERE t1.ZIP = t2.ZIP AND t1.City != t2.City!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Oh, clever! The predicate conjunction inside the negation IS the exact SQL WHERE clause of a dirty-tuple detector!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: And even domain-specific rules like higher tax brackets cannot earn lower net salaries translate straight into SQL Denial Constraints automatically!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Wait a second, Dr. Nova—I always assumed NFKC normalization in Python handled every messy web copy-paste quirk! Are you saying U+200B Zero-Width Space survives NFKC completely untouched?

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: One hundred percent untouched, Kaito! Zero-width spaces and zero-width joiners carry intentional formatting semantics in Unicode cursive and right-to-left scripts, so the Unicode standard explicitly excludes them from NFKC compatibility folding.

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: So when a user copies their email or username from Slack or a PDF with a hidden U+200B or U+FEFF Byte Order Mark, their profile renders identically on screen—yet SQL join equality fails silently!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Let us inspect those exact invisible hex codepoints live inside our first interactive Canvas lab!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Whoa, Dr. Nova! Look at Trap 1 in the canvas when I click Naive NFKC Only: the fi ligature U+FB01 folds cleanly into f and i, yet that red U+200B block sits stubbornly between e and S—and the SQL Join badge still flashes FAILED!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Now switch to Two-Stage Canonicalize, Kaito, and look at Trap 3 with the BOM header U+FEFF and non-breaking space U+00A0!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Instant green PASS! Superscript 2 normalized to regular ASCII 2, U+00A0 collapsed cleanly to standard ASCII space U+0020, and U+FEFF disappeared completely!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: That two-stage invariant is non-negotiable on every string join key. Test yourself on Active Checkpoint 1 next!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: We just proved this in Lab 1, Dr. Nova! Even though NFKC decomposes compatibility ligatures like fi and converts full-width digits to ASCII, formatting characters like U+200B Zero-Width Space and U+FEFF Byte Order Mark survive NFKC untouched!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Precisely, Kaito! Why don't regular whitespace strippers like Python's dot-strip catch U+200B either?

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: First, U+200B is buried inside the middle of the string, and second, neither NFKC nor default trim strips invisible formatting characters! You have to run an explicit regex removing Unicode range 200B through 200D and FEFF right after NFKC!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Spot on! Lock in Option A below to advance to Module Part 2.

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Dr. Nova, I noticed something clever in our MIMIC-III blood pressure parser: checking Systolic between 50 and 260 plus Diastolic between 30 and 160 rejects broken 999 slash 999 cuff errors—AND catches October 12 written as 10 slash 12 too!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Yes, and look closely at the THIRD guard condition: Systolic strictly greater than Diastolic! What slips past individual min-max range bounds if you forget that inequality, Kaito?

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: A nurse accidentally typing diastolic first and systolic second—like 80 slash 120—or a numeric calendar note like 55 slash 110! Both individual numbers lie comfortably inside 30 to 260, yet physiologically Systolic cannot fall below Diastolic!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Regex extracts candidate syntax; physical inequalities certify semantic truth. Next, let us compare deletion against donor-preserving imputation.

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Dr. Nova, wait—why would Pairwise Available-Case correlation ever produce an invalid non-positive-semi-definite covariance matrix? Isn't every Pearson correlation strictly bounded between minus one and plus one?

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Individually yes, Kaito—yet pairwise deletion mixes DIFFERENT row subsets for every matrix cell! Suppose covariance of X1 and X2 is estimated over patients 1 to 600, while X2 and X3 uses patients 400 to 1,000, and X1 and X3 uses rows 1 to 300!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Because each pair lives on a different subset geometry, they can form mathematically impossible correlation triangles! When you pass that stitched matrix to PCA or Cholesky decomposition, linear algebra explodes with a negative eigenvalue!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Spot on! Completing cells deterministically via 1-NN Hot-Deck donor records guarantees a single coherent n-row matrix before computing any covariance.

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Look closely at those 4 EHR rows, Dr. Nova! Only Patient 101 started cleanly! If someone ran naive listwise deletion, Patients 102, 103, and 104 would ALL get dropped—leaving only 25% of the ward table!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Wait until you notice WHY weighted constraints solve each error without guessing, Kaito: Patient 102 had two peer visits certifying Stanford for 94305; Patient 103's immutable Intake Admit timestamp proves Discharge cannot be Day 7; and Patient 104's unparseable cuff sentinel 999 slash 999 nullifies safely rather than pretending to be blood pressure!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: AND then Patient 104's missing Age matches Patient 101—whose BMI is 24.5 right next to 25.0—giving exact donor Age 45.0 instead of smearing an arbitrary sample average!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: That exact 4-patient scenario awaits in Lab 2 right after we inspect enterprise escalation tiers.

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Dr. Nova, suppose a legacy hospital migration leaves 2,000 ambiguous conflict rows where weights tie evenly—so automated Bohannon repair cannot pick a unique winner safely. Can doctors manually verify all 2,000 charts?

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Never, Kaito—physician review hours are our scarcest resource! That is exactly what Krishnan's ActiveClean framework solves: estimate how strongly cleaning each dirty record shifts your downstream predictor gradient!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: So records deep inside a settled region barely change model decision boundaries, while boundary anomalies near high mortality risk swing gradient norms hugely! Fixing those top 5% delivers 90% of downstream AUC gains!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Deterministic automation handles 99% of dirt at zero labor cost; ActiveClean steers scarce human expertise cleanly onto high-stakes tied conflicts!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Look at that comparison in the studio Canvas below, Dr. Nova! When I switch to Naive Listwise Drop, the red bar drops cohort retention straight down to 25%—only Patient 101 remains!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Now trigger Execute Minimum Modification Repair r star, Kaito! Watch how each attribute weight steers repairs cleanly onto lowest-cost mutable fields.

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Boom! Patient 102 flips Palo Alto to Stanford at cost 1, Patient 103 fixes Discharge from Day 7 to Day 11 at cost 1, Patient 104 nullifies cuff error 999 slash 999 at cost 1 and inherits Age 45 from nearest BMI neighbor P_101! Total cost equals 3.0, zero violations remain, and 100% of patients are preserved!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Now apply that exact cost calculus in Active Checkpoint 2!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Let me calculate all three candidate repairs carefully, Dr. Nova! First: change Record 2's City from Palo Alto to Stanford—that modifies one City cell so cost equals 1 times 1.0 equals 1.0.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: And what about the competing valid repairs?

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Flipping Records 1 and 3 from Stanford to Palo Alto edits two City cells for cost 2.0, while altering Record 2's postal-verified ZIP code costs 5.0! Deletion throws away a patient chart unnecessarily!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Minimum cost 1.0 wins cleanly—and guarantees no negative pairwise eigenvalues downstream! Choose Option A below!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Look at that leap on MIMIC-III, Dr. Nova: dropping unparsed records erased 64% of patients and crippled mortality ROC-AUC at 0.692! Even univariate mean imputation left MSE huge at 142.3!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: And think clinically about WHY complete-case deletion collapsed AUC so badly, Kaito: hurried emergency ICU notes were the exact encounters with shorthand blood pressures and backward billing timestamps! Deleting unparsed charts disproportionately erased the sickest patients!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Which created MNAR selection bias on top of losing two-thirds of training sample size! Declarative regex + 1-NN donor matching lifted coverage to 99.1%, kept 100% cohort retention, and shot ROC-AUC up to 0.838!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Let us translate every single guarantee into our production Pydantic V2 Python verification module next.

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Look how concise and auditable DeclarativeDataCleaner is, Dr. Nova! Every single lesson theorem maps to an explicit method and CI unit assertion!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: And look at the order inside test declarative cleaning assertions: canonicalize text runs BEFORE audit functional dependency, parse blood pressure explicitly rejects both INVALID and 999 slash 999, and NearestNeighbors imputes exact integer Age from validated donors!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Finally, CleaningAuditReport serializes clean Pydantic telemetry straight into production observability logs—catching silent zero-width or timestamp regressions before training starts!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Ready to graduate Chapter 5.5 and preview Feature Scaling and Encoding in Lesson 5.6!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Dr. Nova, linking Unicode bytes, First-Order Denial Constraints, Bohannon weights, and 1-NN Hot-Deck into one coherent pipeline makes complete architectural sense now!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: And remember what MIMIC-III taught us empirically, Kaito: rescuing those messy records without mean-smearing lifted mortality ROC-AUC from 0.692 straight to 0.838!

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Never delete rows blindly, never trust NFKC alone without zero-width stripping, and validate regex extractions inside physical bounds! Ready for Lesson 5.6: Scaling, Centering, and Categorical Encoding!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: See you in Lesson 5.6, Kaito!
